sources.headline: Secret police files released in Hungary, 37 years after fall of communism
sources.text: Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule. Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members. The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution."I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity," Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest."Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer. Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided. Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary. Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power."In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party. Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

sources.headline: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files
sources.text:
On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.In 1956, Hungarians tried to stop Soviet tanks with cobble stone barricades Image: AP Photo/picture alliance
Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.Release opposed for years
Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.
Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.
A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.
The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.
Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.Viktor Orban's Fidesz party never supported making the 'agent files' publicImage: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance
One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Political fallout expected
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.
Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.
The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.
Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.
Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."Defendants are questioned by a judge in Budapest on March 9, 1957, during the first show trial held after the 1956 Hungarian uprisingImage: MTI/picture alliance
Political reckoning
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.
When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.
Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

sources.headline: Hungary: communist-era files released, up to 60,000 former agents revealed
sources.text:
In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.
Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time.
"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives.
"For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said.
Public figures featured in registry
Politicians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive.
The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations.
"Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity."
Various types of documents disclosed
Under the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone.
On Wednesday morning, the three of these became accessible on the nyitottaktak.hu (source in Hungarian) website.
The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member.
A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.
The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.
A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.
Around 150,000 agents during communist era
Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.
Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.
Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.
Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.
But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office.
Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.
Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete.
'Better late than never'
Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.
The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.
The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation.
"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.
But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants.
"I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

sources.headline: Hungary's former PM Orban says he rebuffed secret police recruitment
sources.text: BUDAPEST, Nov 3 - Hungary's former Prime Minister Viktor Orban said on Tuesday that Communist secret services had tried to recruit him as an informer while he was doing his military service but he refused, and that he later became the target of heavy police surveillance.Orban issued a statement on Facebook, along with secret service documents from 1982 and the late 1980s.Hungary is due on Wednesday to start releasing tens of thousands of Communist-era police files in an online public database, giving people access to lists of informers and collaborators used by the former state security services."During the early part of my military service, they attempted to recruit me, but I refused, so the attempt proved unsuccessful," Orban wrote on Facebook."Later, I, my wife, and my fellow opposition members were kept under constant surveillance. We were all targets of the state party’s secret investigations."Orban, whose 16-year nationalist rule ended in an election in April when Prime Minister Peter Magyar's centre-right Tisza party ousted him, said the documents revealed that "informants were set upon us, and listening devices were installed in our workplaces, our homes — and even in our bedrooms."The opening of the archives on Wednesday is part of Magyar's pledge to make the records — stored in a vast basement of archives in Budapest — public and to allow Hungarians to come to terms with their totalitarian past.Although Communist rule ended in 1989, Hungary delayed fully opening the files due to a lack of political will from successive governments. Until now, apart from researchers, ordinary people were only able to request access to their own records or those of close family members. Now anybody will be able to conduct searches in the online database.Between 1956 and 1989, some 55,000 secret collaborators were recorded in Hungary. REUTERS
